question: Over the past eighty years, there has been a steady migration of population from rural areas to urban centres. According to UN data, only 30% of the global population lived in cities in 1950, and the figure is expected to rise to 66% by 2050. Villages are shrinking and disappearing.

Aradena in Sfakia, Kalami and Sfendyli near Heraklion, Kranionas in Kastoria, Eleousa on the island of Rhodes, Palia Plagia in Aitoloakarnania, Mavronoros (Ioannina) and Gavros (Koresteia) are some of the Greek villages that for economic, geological or historical reasons, have been completely abandoned.

Architectural masterpieces and ways of life are being forgotten and swept aside as time and technology overtake them. Mass industrialisation and job opportunities in the cities may threaten the viability of rural life, while on the other hand, urban life is faced with diseconomies of scale, with excessively high rents making life extremely difficult for city dwellers.
Citizens’ demand for a better quality of life outside the cities is growing. Italy, Spain and Portugal have launched initiatives for repopulating abandoned villages. In view of this: 1.
Does the Commission support initiatives for decentralisation?
Is there some form of investment framework, or are some incentives offered for the regions to undertake the repopulation and organised development of abandoned villages?
Are there any available European programmes that Greece could use to revive its abandoned or very small villages?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.9.2024) The Commission pursues actions for achieving economic, social, and territorial cohesion in the EU, one facet of which is supporting multi-pole development and promoting smaller urban centres and rural areas.

In particular, through Cohesion policy, the Commission supports the development of territories with investments based on strategies designed by local authorities to respond to their needs, notably in relation to demographic challenges1. A platform on Harnessing Talent2 is also in place to support EU’s territories to address demographic transition.

The Long-Term vision for EU’s rural areas3 aims at supporting stronger, connected, resilient and prosperous rural areas. It comprises an Action Plan4 which defines the actions undertaken by the Commission to address, among others, demographic issues and the Rural Pact5, a framework for cooperation for rural stakeholders.

For the Cohesion Policy programming period 2021-2027, Greek regions invest in non-urban areas, including villages, to address specific economic and demographic challenges, and reduce inequalities. Under the shared management principle, the project selection in each region is the responsibility of the designated Member State’s authorities.

The Common Agricultural Policy also tackles depopulation, promotes social inclusion and local development in rural areas, through initiatives such as LEADER - community led local development approach and by providing support for setting up of young farmers and new farmers, rural business and start-ups.
1 Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 laying down

common provisions on the European Regional Development Fund, the European Social Fund Plus, the Cohesion Fund, the Just Transition Fund and the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund and financial rules for those and for the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund, the Internal Security Fund and the Instrument for Financial Support for Border Management and Visa Policy http://data.europa.
